content.text: Book reference: Chapter 15, pages 527–556. Guided Exercises: Mounting and Unmounting File Systems, Locating Files on the System. Lab: Accessing Linux File Systems.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This whole chapter
Identifying block devices, mounting/unmounting by UUID, and using find with real search criteria (permissions, size, time, type) are all standard, hands-on RHCSA tasks.

sections.title: 15.1 Block devices and the file-system hierarchy

content.text: Linux presents every storage device's contents as part of one single directory tree, rather than separate drive letters — a file system on any device becomes visible by being mounted onto an existing (normally empty) directory called its mount point. Once mounted, ls on that directory shows the mounted file system's contents, indistinguishable in normal use from any other directory.
NOTE — Not like Windows drive letters

This is closer to NTFS "mounted folders" than to drive letters — you generally don't need to know or care which physical device a file lives on, until you need to check free space, investigate a hardware error, or determine whether two files can be hard-linked (which requires being on the same file system).
Block device naming
Storage type
Whole-disk naming
Partition naming
SATA/SAS/USB
/dev/sda, /dev/sdb...
/dev/sda1, /dev/sdb3...
virtio-blk (many VMs)
/dev/vda, /dev/vdb...
/dev/vda1, /dev/vdb3...
NVMe SSDs
/dev/nvme0, /dev/nvme1...
/dev/nvme0p1, /dev/nvme1p3...
SD/MMC cards
/dev/mmcblk0...
/dev/mmcblk0p1...
NOTE —

Many virtual machines (including ones built the way this guide's Part 0 does) actually use the newer virtio-scsi paravirtualized driver, which shows up with ordinary /dev/sd*-style names rather than /dev/vd* — check with lsblk rather than assuming from the hypervisor alone.
ls -l on any of these shows file type b (block device) as the very first character — e.g. brw-rw----. 1 root disk 8, 1 ... /dev/sda1.
Partitions vs. LVM

A disk can be divided into partitions (fixed, simple divisions) or organized with LVM (Logical Volume Management), which pools one or more block devices into a volume group, then carves that pool into logical volumes that behave like partitions but can be resized far more flexibly. A logical volume named mylv in volume group myvg appears as /dev/myvg/mylv — actually a symbolic link to the real underlying device file, which can vary between boots; /dev/mapper/ contains an equivalent, also-symlinked naming scheme you'll also encounter.
Checking space usage
Command
Shows
df
Every mounted file system: total, used, available space, percent used
df -h
Same, in binary-prefix human-readable units (KiB/MiB/GiB, powers of 1024)
df -H
Same, in SI units (KB/MB/GB, powers of 1000 — what drive manufacturers advertise in)
du /path
Recursive size of everything under a directory tree, file by file
du -h /path
Same, human-readable
⚠ WARNING — df -h and df -H report different numbers for the same disk — neither is wrong

A "1 TB" drive as advertised (SI, powers of 1000) shows as roughly 931 GiB under df -h (binary, powers of 1024) — same physical capacity, two legitimate but different counting conventions. Don't mistake this gap for missing disk space.
tmpfs and devtmpfs entries in df output are memory-backed, not disk-backed — their contents vanish on every reboot, which is expected behavior, not data loss.
Command
Shows
lsblk
Every block device, its size, and current mount point (if any), in a tree showing partition/LVM relationships
lsblk -fp
Adds full device path, file-system type, and UUID — the command to run before mounting anything by UUID
mount /dev/vdb1 /mnt/data # mount by device name
mount UUID="46f543fd-78c9-4526-a857-244811be2d88" /mnt/data # mount by UUID
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Mount by UUID, not device name, whenever it matters

Device names like /dev/sdb1 depend on detection order, which can shift if disks are added, removed, or a controller enumerates them differently after a reboot — the exact problem persistent interface naming solved for networking in Chapter 12. A file system's UUID is embedded in the file system itself and never changes on its own, making it the reliable identifier for anything beyond a quick, temporary mount.

The destination directory must already exist before mounting. /mnt exists by default specifically for temporary mount points; for anything longer-lived, a purpose-named subdirectory (or a location elsewhere in the hierarchy) is more common.
⚠ WARNING — Mounting onto a non-empty directory hides its existing contents

Any files already present in that directory become completely inaccessible (not deleted — just hidden underneath the newly mounted file system) until you unmount it again. This is a common source of "my files disappeared" confusion that resolves itself the moment you unmount.
Unmounting
umount /mnt/data
⚠ WARNING — "target is busy" almost always means a shell's current directory

The single most common cause: some process (very often just your own shell, via cd) has its working directory somewhere inside the mount point. cd out of it (or cd with no arguments, to go home) and retry. lsof /mnt/data lists every process with open files there if the cause isn't your own shell — from there you can wait for the process to finish, or send it SIGTERM/SIGKILL if appropriate.

Removable media is unmounted automatically as part of a normal shutdown/reboot, which also flushes any data still cached in memory to disk. Pulling a USB drive WITHOUT unmounting it first risks exactly that cached, not-yet-written data being lost or the file system being left in an inconsistent state.
In a graphical session, removable media auto-mounts at /run/media/USERNAME/LABEL — LABEL being the volume's own name if it has one.
NOTE — Persistent mounts (surviving reboot) are RH134 territory

This book doesn't cover /etc/fstab (the file that makes a mount permanent across reboots) at the RH124 level — every mount command above is a manual, one-time mount that won't survive a restart. fstab-based persistent mounting is part of the follow-on RH134 course.
Tool
How it works
Trade-off
locate
Looks up a pre-built index (the mlocate database)
Instant, but can be stale — misses anything created since the last index update
find
Crawls the real file system live, right now
Always accurate, but slower on a large tree
locate
locate passwd # substring match anywhere in the name or path
locate -i messages # case-insensitive
locate -n 5 snow.png # limit to the first 5 results
sudo updatedb # force an immediate index rebuild (normally runs once a day automatically)
⚠ WARNING — locate can't find what its index doesn't know about yet

A file created moments ago won't show up in locate results until the next updatedb run (daily by default) — if a search should find something but doesn't, that's the first thing to suspect, not a broken locate installation.

Access is also filtered by permission: locate only reveals a path to a user who actually has search (execute) permission on every directory in that path — it can't be used to discover the existence of files you couldn't otherwise reach.
find — the real-time, criteria-rich search tool
NOTE — find's option syntax is genuinely unusual

Unlike most commands, find's options come AFTER the path argument, and long-form options still use a single dash (-name, not --name). This trips up people used to normal GNU option conventions — it's simply how find has always worked.
find / -name sshd_config # exact name match, from / down
find / -name '*.txt' # wildcard — MUST be quoted, or the shell expands it before find ever sees it
find / -iname '*messages*' # case-insensitive
Searching by ownership
Option
Matches
-user NAME / -group NAME
Owning user / group, by name
-uid N / -gid N
Owning user / group, by numeric ID
-user and -group can combine in one command — find / -user root -group mail finds files owned by root specifically with group ownership mail, useful for spotting an unusual owner/group combination.
Searching by permission — the exam-relevant one to drill
Prefix
Matches files where...
(none) e.g. -perm 764
Permissions are EXACTLY this value
- e.g. -perm -324
ALL of the specified bits are set (others may also be set)
/ e.g. -perm /442
AT LEAST ONE of the specified bits is set, in any category
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Drill this distinction with real permission strings, not just in the abstract

Try it yourself against a file you can see with ls -l: -perm -222 requires ALL three write bits (user, group, AND other) to be set — rw-r--r-- fails this, since only the owner has write. -perm /222 requires AT LEAST ONE of those same three write bits — rw-r--r-- passes this, since the owner's write bit alone is enough. Same three digits, opposite prefix, very different match. Practice converting a handful of real ls -l outputs against both prefixes until the distinction is automatic — it's easy to get backwards under exam time pressure.
Searching by size and time
Option
Example
Matches
-size
-size +10G / -size -10k / -size 10M
Larger than / smaller than / approximately this size (k/M/G — rounds UP to the nearest unit)
-mmin
-mmin 120 / -mmin +200 / -mmin -150
Content modified exactly / more than / less than N minutes ago
⚠ WARNING — -size rounds up — a 1-byte file matches -size 1M

find -size 1M actually matches every file from just over 0 bytes up to 1 MB, because find rounds file sizes UP to the nearest whole unit before comparing. This surprises people expecting an exact-size match.
Searching by type and link count
-type value
Matches
f
Regular file
d
Directory
l
Soft (symbolic) link
b
Block device
-links +1 finds files with MORE than one hard link — i.e. files that have at least one additional hard-linked name somewhere, tying directly back to Chapter 3's hard-link concept.

All of find's criteria combine in a single command — e.g. find /home -type f -perm -002 -size +10M finds world-writable regular files over 10 MB, a genuinely useful real security-audit query, not just a syntax exercise.

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. lsblk on servera — identify every disk and partition, and which (if any) are currently mounted.
2. lsblk -fp — note the UUID of your root file system.
3. df -h and df -H on the same system — compare the two reported sizes for the same partition and confirm you understand why they differ.
4. du -h /var/log | tail -5 — see which subdirectories of /var/log are using the most space.
5. locate passwd, then touch ~/newtestfile.txt and immediately locate newtestfile — confirm it does NOT show up yet, then sudo updatedb and locate again to confirm it now does.
6. find /etc -name '*.conf' | wc -l — count configuration files under /etc.
7. find /home -type f -perm -002 — hunt for any world-writable regular files under /home (there shouldn't be any on a stock system — a good sanity check).
8. find / -mmin -60 -type f 2>/dev/null | head -20 — files modified in the last hour, discarding permission-denied noise.
1. Q1 — You created a file two minutes ago and locate can't find it, but find can. Why the difference, and what command fixes locate's blind spot immediately rather than waiting?
2. Q2 — umount /mnt/data fails with "target is busy." What's the single most common cause, and the fastest fix?
3. Q3 — Why is mounting by UUID generally preferred over mounting by device name like /dev/sdb1?
NOTE — Answers

Q1 — locate searches a pre-built index (the mlocate database) that only refreshes once a day by default, so a file created minutes ago simply isn't in it yet; find searches the live file system in real time, so it always sees current state. sudo updatedb forces an immediate index rebuild instead of waiting for the daily schedule.

Q2 — Almost always: some process — very often your own shell — has its current working directory inside the mount point. cd out of it (or cd with no arguments) and retry; if that's not it, lsof /mnt/data shows exactly which process is holding it open.

Q3 — Device names like /dev/sdb1 are assigned based on detection order, which can shift if disks are added, removed, or enumerated differently after a reboot. A file system's UUID is embedded in the file system itself and stays constant regardless of detection order, making it the reliable choice for anything beyond a quick, temporary mount.

Storage devices appear as block devices under /dev (/dev/sd*, /dev/vd*, /dev/nvme*...); partitions and LVM logical volumes are both block devices in their own right, with a mounted file system's contents joined into the single directory tree at its mount point.
df (and -h/-H for human-readable binary vs. SI units) reports space by file system; du reports space recursively by directory tree.

lsblk -fp identifies devices and their UUIDs; mount UUID=... (preferred over device names, which can shift) attaches a file system, umount detaches it — "target is busy" almost always means a process's current directory is still inside the mount point.

locate is instant but relies on a once-daily index (updatedb refreshes it immediately if needed); find searches live and supports rich criteria — name/-iname, -user/-group/-uid/-gid, -perm (exact / - all-of / + at-least-one-of), -size (rounds up), -mmin, and -type — all combinable in a single command.
